transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-29 16:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording)
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Ortiz (Cascade Clinical), Samir Patel (IT Ops), Joan Rivers (Security & Compliance), Marcus Lee (Infra)

Summary:
Cascade Clinical is evaluating an air-gapped / sealed-facility private deployment for inference of clinical NLP models. Primary concerns: offline update process, hardware footprint and cost, patching windows, operator access, HSM/KMS integration for keys, and audit evidence for regulators. Customer wants a plan that avoids cloud egress for PHI and minimizes operator interaction.

Topics covered:
- Deployment options: fully air-gapped private vs dedicated hosted fallback
- Update mechanisms: removable media, signed artifacts, secure transfer procedures
- Hardware: GPU choices (A100 vs A40 vs H100), CPU/memory, storage IO
- Security controls: KMS/HSM, RBAC, SSO, audit logs, SOC2/ISO mapping
- Ops: patch windows, rollback, model pinning/versioning, model size/quantization tradeoffs
- Next steps: run perf estimates, share checklist, schedule on-site compliance deep-dive

Action items (recorded in notes):
- Priya to run throughput estimate for candidate hardware; Alex to share checklist; Marcus to provide patch windows; Joan to share compliance matrix.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone thanks for carving out time, really appreciate it. Our goal for today is to understand the sealed facility requirements and any non-negotiables so we can map to Redwood Private. Priya and I will capture technical and compliance constraints.
[00:22] Dr. Elena (Cascade): Thanks Alex. To be blunt, we cannot have any egress of PHI to public cloud. Some models can live in a non-sensitive environment but our core clinical annotator models must be wholly contained. We also have strict change control windows.
[00:40] Priya (Redwood-SE): Understood. Quick clarifying question — when you say sealed, do you mean no outbound network at all from the inference nodes, or only restricted outbound to an internal management VLAN?
[00:55] Samir (IT Ops): No outbound to the internet. Management plane is on the same airgapped fabric. We can have a jump host in a DMZ that faciliated signed artifact ingestion but that box is offline to the internet except for manual USB loading.
[01:15] Alex: Great, that maps to typical air-gap scenarios we see. We support private control planes running in-customer and offline update workflows. The key pieces to validate are: how you want updates delivered (signed tarballs, hardware-locked tokens), who can perform updates, and what evidence auditors expect.
[01:35] Joan (Security): For auditors we need a chain of custody for model updates, cryptographic signatures, and HSM-backed key management. Also need an immutable audit trail for inference requests tied to RBAC identities.
[01:52] Priya: Quick note — our runtime can be configured to use a customer-managed KMS/HSM for model keys, and we can ship signed model artifacts. In air-gap setups customers often bring their own HSM appliance or use an on-prem KMS.
[02:08] Marcus (Infra): Ok that sounds fine. On hardware, what are typical GPU counts for a production deploy of the 7B clinical annotator? It spikes on long sequence lengths (1.5–2k tokens).
[02:28] Priya: Roughly speaking for low-latency serving with a 2k seq, you'll look at A100 80GB class for best perf, or an H100 if you want headroom. For batchy throughput we can do A40s but it depends on latency SLOs. I'll run a more concrete estimate.
[02:50] Dr. Elena: Latency SLO is 300–400ms P95 for single-turn inference. Throughput is around 150–250 requests/hour with bursts.
[03:05] Alex: Noted. That small request volume helps. We should be able to meet that with 2–4 A100s depending on token distribution and KV cache behavior.
[03:22] Samir: About KV cache — we can't persist anything unencrypted. Is the KV cache stored in RAM only? If it spills to disk, we need disk encryption and document how it's wiped.
[03:38] Priya: The typical config keeps KV cache in RAM, but for very long contexts we may checkpoint; we can disable checkpointing. We also support encrypted swap and we can show where the cache lives. Sometimes the transcription shows k-v cash which is hilarious.
[03:52] Alex: *laughs* Yeah, transcriptions.
[03:56] Joan: Another non-negotiable: only vetted operators can mount media on the jump host. We need signed manifests and role separation — developer cannot initiate an update without operations producing an attestation.
[04:12] Priya: We can support a signed manifest flow where the build system signs models and the operations team validates signature during manual ingest. We also support an allowlist of operator identities via RBAC.
[04:26] Dr. Elena: Can Redwood handle canary rollouts on-prem? We want to deploy a new model to a small subset of nodes first then roll forward.
[04:37] Priya: Yes — Redwood Private supports rollout policies including canary, A/B, and automatic rollback on error thresholds. In air-gap mode the controller runs locally so the policy enforcement is local. The only manual step is the artifact transfer if the site is fully offline.
[04:55] Marcus: Patch windows — we do weekly maintenance windows on Saturdays 02:00–06:00. Any updates must be packaged and consumable within that window, or staged for the next night.
[05:09] Alex: We'll capture that. In practice our update payloads are small when only model deltas are used; but initial model syncs can be large (tens to hundreds of GB). Do you have constraints around physical transfer sizes?
[05:25] Samir: On initial seed we can accept a secured hard drive via courier. For incremental updates, smaller signed bundles on encrypted thumb drives preferred.
[05:36] Dr. Elena: About keys — HSM integration is required for signing operations and key storage. Can Redwood integrate with HSM vendors like Thales and Vault HSM?
[05:48] Priya: We have integrations with customer-managed Vault, PKCS#11-compatible HSMs, and some appliances. We'll need specifics for the exact vendor but the design is compatible. We'll note potential dependencies in the runbook.
[06:05] Alex: Curious — have you evaluated a hybrid approach where non-PHI models are hosted in Redwood Dedicated while PHI models stay on-prem?
[06:16] Dr. Elena: Yes, we looked at that. There's appetite for hybrid, but legal wants a clear boundary and docs proving no model drift or data leakage across the environments. That gets tricky.
[06:30] Joan: Anything that touches PHI must be auditable and isolated. If hybrid is used, strict network and authentication boundaries must be enforced and tested in our SOC audits.
[06:42] Priya: We can document separation and routing policies, and provide test harnesses for certification.
[06:48] Alex: For timelines — what's your target for a POC/pilot?
[06:52] Dr. Elena: We'd like a POC in 6–8 weeks, pilot in Q1 2027 if everything lines up.
[06:59] Alex: That seems doable. Priya, we'll need to scope the POC hardware and an acceptance criteria doc.
[07:05] Priya: I'll prepare a perf matrix that maps A40/A100/H100 options to your latency/throughput profile and supply a recommended config plus a conservative and cost-optimized option.
[07:18] Samir: Also to note — our airgap environment has no external DNS resolution. Any service discovery must be via IP/hosts or a local registry.
[07:29] Priya: Redwood Private supports static registries and can run a local control plane. No cloud callbacks required.
[07:36] Marcus: On backup/restore: we can allow backups to internal backup appliance but cannot send backups offsite without encryption and approval. What's Redwood's backup story for models and KV cache?
[07:48] Priya: Models are immutable artifacts; you can store them in your internal artifact repo. Runtime state like KV cache is ephemeral by default; we don't recommend backup of caches. We can provide a documented restore path for model artifacts and controller state.
[08:06] Dr. Elena: About licensing — are we buying a per-token usage license for private or a flat site license? Pricing model will affect procurement timelines.
[08:18] Alex: Pricing for Private is typically a license plus support tier and optional reserved hardware. For air-gap we usually do an enterprise agreement covering the site and number of supported GPUs. I'll share a ballpark so procurement can start.
[08:32] Joan: We also require red team testing and a runbook for incident response that shows how to revoke keys and rollback models.
[08:41] Priya: We can provide a sample incident playbook and include procedures for key revocation and model rollback in the runbook.
[08:51] Alex: Two practical questions — is there an on-site systems integrator you use for hardware procurement, or will Cascade source machines directly?
[08:59] Marcus: We have a preferred vendor list but procurement can work with Redwood if needed. We'll share the approved vendor list.
[09:08] Priya: Noted. We'll ensure configurations match vendor images and drivers.
[09:15] Dr. Elena: Any gotchas with quantization? If we quantize to reduce GPU memory we must verify clinical accuracy.
[09:25] Priya: Absolutely — quantization can change output distribution. We recommend doing an eval against your held-out clinical prompts. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles and we can attach evaluation metrics to any change so you have regression alerts.
[09:41] Samir: About observability — we need per-request audit tokens, per-route latency and cost attribution for chargeback.
[09:51] Alex: Redwood Console supports token-level and route-level cost/latency breakdowns and exports logs to your SIEM. In air-gap mode, exports go to your local logging endpoint.
[10:05] Joan: Is there any telemetry that leaves the site by default? We must veto that.
[10:11] Priya: No telemetry leaves by default. Any telemetry export is opt-in and configurable to your internal endpoints.
[10:18] Dr. Elena: Ok this is useful. I think next steps are clear. We'll wait for the checklist and perf numbers and then schedule the on-site compliance deep-dive.
[10:29] Alex: Great. We'll also include examples of signed manifest flows and a sample artifact package for review. I'll follow up with the deck and SOC2 snapshot after the call.
[10:40] Marcus: One last ops note — we require that any root-level changes are done under a service window with two-person authorization. Can rollouts be gated?
[10:50] Priya: Yes, rollouts can require approvals. The local control plane enforces RBAC and can require multiple approvers for canary promotion.
[10:58] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll recapitulate action items in an email after the call.
[11:04] Dr. Elena: Thanks.
